title: David's last words (2 Samuel 23:1–4)
hook: one who rules justly is "as the light of the morning"

segments.voice: Yesterday the wise woman on Abel's wall called for the commander and saved her town. Your line was one wise voice saves a city. Today, near the end of Samuel, David's own voice, in a poem.

After the rooftop, the ewe lamb, the child, Tamar, the climb, the cry over the gate, the book gives David a short poem and calls it his last words. It opens like a signature. David the son of Jesse says. The man raised up on high says. The anointed of the God of Jacob. The sweet singer of Israel. Then he says where the words come from: the spirit of the Lord spoke by me, and his word was on my tongue. What he passes on is a picture of what a ruler should be.
screen: `AFTER EVERYTHING, A POEM.` → `THE SON OF JESSE SAYS.` → `HIS WORD WAS ON MY TONGUE.`

segments.voice: The God of Israel said, the Rock of Israel spoke to me: one who rules over people must be just, ruling in the fear of God. Then the image. He shall be "as the light of the morning, when the sun riseth", a morning without clouds, like tender grass springing out of the earth by clear shining after rain. Justice in this poem isn't a sword or a gavel. It's daylight. Morning light doesn't choose whose field to shine on. A fair ruler, read this way, lets everyone underneath grow. Now hold that next to the man saying it: the king who took another man's wife, arranged a death, heard what was done to his daughter Tamar and, as far as the text says, did nothing, and whose own son rose against him. The poem erases none of that. Beside his story, it reads as an ideal his own life shows is hard to reach. The next line can be heard two ways. Some translations have David admit that his house is not so with God; the Jewish translation of 1917 hears a question: is not my house so with God? Either way, the line ends on an everlasting covenant God has made with him. One honest note: the opening of the book of Kings records later instructions from David to Solomon. Perhaps these are his last words as a poet, or the book's chosen farewell. Either way, the words it labels last are not about battles. They are about light.
screen: `RULING JUSTLY, IN THE FEAR OF GOD.` · then, large: `AS THE LIGHT OF THE MORNING.` · then: `GRASS AFTER RAIN.` · `AN IDEAL HE REACHED FOR.`

segments.voice: You're in charge of something, even if it's small: a household, a team, a classroom, a dog. Picture the people in it and ask whether someone gets less of your light: less patience, less benefit of the doubt. If you pray, you can hold David's picture: the light of the morning.
Sweet singer. One title David gives himself in his last poem, before describing what a just ruler looks like. Today's word.
Your line: like the light of morning. Looking back on the week: Tamar, lev, barefoot, Shimei, O Absalom, the wise woman, and the sweet singer. Day seven hundred fifty-six, done.

howItsDone: Jews read David's last words as part of the book of Samuel; David is remembered in Jewish tradition as the sweet singer of Israel, and some psalms carry his name in their headings.

Strong in battle, like a sword that keeps every enemy far away.
Feared by all, like a storm that keeps the people in their place.

'His house is not so with God, yet an everlasting covenant' paraphrases 23:5, whose sense is debated (statement or question); the script offers two readings.
